strengths: Identifies and formalizes an important, practically relevant and previously underexplored problem: continual (sequential) unlearning in text-to-image diffusion models, with a clear three-requirement definition (erasure, preservation of prior unlearning, retention of unrelated abilities).

Systematic empirical study with a well-motivated evaluation protocol built on UnlearnCanvas, using standardized classifiers for UA/RA-I/RA-C rather than heterogeneous CLIP-similarity or subjective metrics; covers two representative unlearning methods (ConAbl, EraseDiff) and two unlearning domains (styles, objects), with complementary results for EraseDiff in the appendix.

Provides a convincing causal diagnosis: the empirical finding that cumulative parameter drift is much larger under sequential than simultaneous unlearning, supported by a clean Taylor-expansion argument and an empirical estimate of the smoothness constant showing the retention loss lies in a flat basin.

The analysis-driven progression from generic regularizers (L1/L2, selective fine-tuning, TIES merging) to the semantic-aware gradient projection is well structured; the finding that in-domain retention correlates strongly with text-embedding similarity (r = -0.627) and the k,v-update-norm correlation (r = 0.835) give concrete mechanistic motivation for the projection method operating on cross-attention K/V matrices.

The proposed gradient projection is plug-and-play (no knowledge of the retain set), shown to be complementary/compatible with the other regularizers, and is evaluated on both unlearning backbones; benefits grow with sequence length, supporting the continual-setting framing.
Honest positioning: the paper frames itself as a study + baselines rather than overclaiming a novel algorithm, which is appropriate for its contribution.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of the individual components: L1/L2 drift regularization, first-order Taylor bounds, selective fine-tuning, TIES-Merging, and gradient projection (closely related to GEM/OGD-style projection, e.g., Lopez-Paz & Ranzato 2017, Chaudhry et al. 2018) are all well-established continual-learning techniques repurposed here; the methodological contribution rests mostly on the semantic-auxiliary-concept subspace design, which itself is relatively incremental.

Evaluation scope is narrow: a single model (a fine-tuned Stable Diffusion checkpoint from UnlearnCanvas) and a single benchmark, with sequences of only 12 concepts; no evidence of generalization to other architectures (e.g., SDXL), other unlearning methods, longer horizons, or realistic request distributions.

The semantic-similarity analysis (Figure 7) is conducted for a single unlearned concept ("Abstractionism"); the claimed generality of the correlation between embedding similarity and retention loss is supported by only one target concept in the main text, raising concerns about cherry-picking.

Missing comparisons against directly relevant continual-learning baselines (e.g., EWC/SI as principled importance-weighted regularization, A-GEM as gradient projection) beyond the authors' own L1/L2/SelFT/Merge variants, making it hard to judge whether the semantic-aware projection is genuinely needed versus any standard CL regularizer.

Theoretical contribution is thin: the Taylor/Lipschitz bound is a standard restatement, Lemma 7.1 is trivial, and the link between the bound and the proposed projection is informal; no guarantee is given that projecting the gradient does not degrade unlearning of the target itself, and the effect of the projection on UA (vs. retention) is not analyzed theoretically or ablated systematically.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in the main text: number of random sequences/seeds, variance or error bars across sampled sequences, hyperparameter (λ, k%, M auxiliary concepts) selection, and compute costs are deferred or unstated; whether results are averaged over multiple random orderings is unclear.

The held-out auxiliary-concept generation by an LLM introduces a potential confound: the quality/coverage of the auxiliary concept set likely affects projection performance, but no sensitivity analysis of M or filtering threshold is provided in the main paper.

Some figures and claims (e.g., Figure 8's harmonic means, Figure 9's normalized deltas) lack absolute baselines or variance, and the RA-I of even the best methods remains low at later requests, so the paper arguably establishes the problem more convincingly than it solves it.

strengths: The problem of continual (sequential) unlearning for text-to-image diffusion models is well-motivated and largely underexplored; framing it via UA / RA-I / RA-C and extending UnlearnCanvas into a sequence-based benchmark is a useful community contribution.

The empirical diagnosis is convincing: the drift analysis (Figure 4) showing that sequential unlearning accumulates far larger parameter displacement than simultaneous or independent unlearning is a clear, interpretable finding, and the correlation between text-embedding similarity and retention degradation (Figure 7a/b) is a genuinely interesting observation.

The study is reasonably comprehensive in scope: two unlearning algorithms (ConAbl, EraseDiff), both style- and object-level sequences, multiple add-on mechanisms, and compatibility experiments, with supporting results in the appendix.
The methods are plug-and-play and clearly described, making the work reproducible in spirit and directly reusable by practitioners.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: every proposed component is a known technique repurposed. L1/L2 norm regularization, selective fine-tuning (adopted directly from Nguyen et al., 2024), and TIES-Merging (Yadav et al., 2023) are off-the-shelf; the gradient projection is essentially classical gradient episodic memory (GEM) / orthogonal gradient projection applied to W_K, W_V, and is close in spirit to the cited Wu et al. (2025b) 'concept preserving gradient,' which is neither compared against nor clearly differentiated.

The theoretical contribution is superficial. The main 'bound' is a routine second-order Taylor expansion with Cauchy–Schwarz, and Lemma 7.1 is trivial. Moreover, the lemma is loosely stated: it concerns gradient vectors in embedding space, but the updates are applied to projection matrices W_K/W_V, so the claimed first-order invariance does not rigorously establish what the paper asserts about parameter updates. There is also an apparent typo ('g' = (I − P_S)g'' should read g⋆), which undermines care in the formalism.

Evaluation is narrow: a single fine-tuned SD checkpoint, one random sequence of 12 concepts (unclear whether multiple sequences/seeds are averaged, and no variance reported), and evaluation solely via classifier accuracy. No image-quality metrics (FID, CLIP score), no human evaluation, and no hyperparameter sensitivity analysis for the regularizer weights (λ), top-k% in SelFT, pruning ratio, or number of auxiliary concepts M.
Missing important baselines: continual-learning methods such as EWC, SI, or GEM applied directly to this setting, and the aforementioned Wu et al. (2025b), are natural comparisons that are absent.

The 'first systematic study' claim is somewhat overstated given Heng & Soh (2023) on continual forgetting in generative models and concurrent LLM merging-for-unlearning work the authors themselves cite; positioning should be more careful.

Reported gains, while consistent, are modest in absolute terms (e.g., harmonic means of 37.8 → 89.6 only in the most favorable combination), and the method underperforms simpler alternatives on RA-C in the object setting, suggesting the practical win is narrower than the abstract implies.

The gradient-projection subspace relies on LLM-generated auxiliary concepts filtered by similarity, introducing an unexamined sensitivity to prompt engineering and to the assumption that embedding-space closeness predicts interference—plausible but supported only by correlations on one concept ('Abstractionism').

strengths: Clear and timely problem formulation: the paper introduces continual unlearning (CU) for text-to-image diffusion models, a realistic and previously underexplored setting (sequential removal requests), and articulates it with a precise definition (erasure, prior-unlearning preservation, retention).

Well-motivated diagnosis: the paper provides a coherent empirical story linking sequential-unlearning failure to cumulative parameter drift (Figure 4), contrasting sequential vs. simultaneous vs. independent unlearning, which is a genuinely useful insight for the community.

Comprehensive experimental design: a benchmark extending UNLEARNCANVAS with style and object unlearning sequences, standardized classifier-based metrics (UA, RA-I, RA-C), two representative unlearning methods (ConAbl, EraseDiff), and results in the appendix for EraseDiff that replicate the main findings.

Useful theoretical framing: a Taylor-expansion/Lipschitz-type bound connecting retention-loss change to parameter drift, plus empirical estimation of curvature, gives the empirical observations a principled (if standard) justification.

The semantic-awareness analysis (negative correlation between text-embedding similarity and retention accuracy, and its link to W_K/W_V cross-attention projections) is a concrete, insightful contribution that motivates the gradient-projection method, which shows clear RA-I gains and compatibility with other regularizers.

The paper is honest about its scope (add-on enhancements rather than a new algorithm) and the methods are plug-and-play, increasing practical utility; reproducibility seems reasonable given the public UNLEARNCANVAS backbone and stated protocols.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of individual components: L1/L2 norm regularization, selective fine-tuning via first-order Taylor importance, TIES-merging, and gradient projection onto an orthogonal complement are all well-established techniques (from continual learning, pruning, and model merging), applied here mostly off-the-shelf. The main contribution is the study and combination, not new methodology; the gradient-projection idea closely mirrors GEM/A-GEM-style constrained updates, and Lemma 7.1 is trivial.

Statistical rigor is thin: sequences are described as 'randomly sampled' but it is unclear how many random orderings were used, and the curves in Figures 3, 6, and 9 lack error bars or variance reporting, making the differences between regularizers (which can be small) hard to assess.

Missing natural baselines from continual learning: despite citing EWC, Synaptic Intelligence, MAS, and replay-based methods as relevant, the paper evaluates only generic L1/L2 penalties. Fisher/parameter-importance-based regularizers and simple replay-based unlearning are conspicuous omissions that weaken the 'regularization perspective' claim.

Evaluation is confined to a single checkpoint/setting (fine-tuned SD on UNLEARNCANVAS) and classifier-based accuracy metrics; there is no human evaluation or FID/CLIP-quality assessment, which is problematic given the paper's claims about 'degraded images' and image quality collapse (Figure 1 is anecdotal).

The theoretical analysis is loose: the Taylor bound is standard, the argument that Hessian terms are 'small' near the optimum is empirical and coarse, and the bound does not formally connect drift to the UA/RA metrics actually reported, so the theory is more motivational than predictive.

Important implementation details and ablations are deferred or missing: the choices of lambda (L1/L2), k% (SelFT), pruning/merge hyperparameters of TIES, M and selection of auxiliary concepts for projection, and sensitivity to these are not characterized in the main text; the cost of the 'simultaneous' upper-bound baseline (which re-unlearns everything per request) is acknowledged but not systematically quantified in the main results.

Scale of the study is modest: 12-concept sequences, one benchmark, two base unlearning algorithms; the generality of the 'utility collapse' phenomenon and of the remedies beyond these conditions remains to be established.

strengths: Timely and clearly motivated problem: continual unlearning for text-to-image diffusion models is a realistic and underexplored setting, and the paper positions it well against both the unlearning and continual learning literatures.

Well-defined setup: the CU problem is formalized with clear requirements (erasure of new targets, preservation of prior unlearning, retention of unrelated capabilities) and sensible metrics (UA, RA-I, RA-C) that distinguish in-domain vs. cross-domain retention — an insightful split.

Convincing root-cause analysis: the paper empirically connects sequential unlearning failure to cumulative parameter drift (Figure 4), supports it with a Taylor-expansion/Lipschitz bound, and validates the smoothness assumption with curvature estimation (Appendix B).

The semantic-aware analysis is a genuine insight: the negative correlation between retention accuracy and text-embedding similarity (Figure 7a), together with the cross-attention (W_K, W_V) mechanism explanation, is well motivated and leads naturally to the gradient-projection method.

Broad experimental coverage: two unlearning methods (ConAbl, SculpMem) plus ESD on SDXL, three erasure domains (styles, objects, celebrities), controls for the early-stopping confound (Appendix D), and analysis of training cost trade-offs (Appendix E).
Useful additional analyses (anchor-driven updates in Figure 9, all-or-nothing erasure under interpolation in Appendix C) that will inform future method design beyond the specific methods proposed.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: all proposed remedies are direct adaptations of existing continual learning techniques (L1/L2 weight regularization, saliency-based selective fine-tuning, TIES-Merging, GEM-style gradient projection onto an orthogonal complement). The gradient-projection twist is the use of LLM-generated auxiliary concepts, but the underlying mechanism is standard.

The theoretical contribution is thin: the bound is a routine second-order Taylor expansion with Cauchy-Schwarz, and the empirical curvature estimate (Figure 18, Spearman p=0.2) provides only weak statistical support for the 'smooth basin' claim.

Hyperparameter sensitivity of the gradient-projection method (number of auxiliary concepts M, similarity filtering threshold, top-k% for SelFT/pruning, regularization strengths) is not systematically ablated in the main text, making it hard to assess robustness of the gains.

Evaluation relies almost entirely on the UnlearnCanvas classifier-based protocol; there is no human evaluation of generated image quality in the main settings, and FID/CLIP-score retention metrics appear only in the celebrity appendix. Classifier-based RA may not fully capture perceptual degradation shown qualitatively in Figure 1.

Limited scale and variance reporting: sequences of only 12 (or 6) concepts, with a single random sequence per setting and no error bars or multiple-sequence variance; robustness to sequence ordering is not assessed despite order being central to the continual setting.
No clear reproducibility statement or code release (the 'Project Page' link is empty), which is a notable gap for a benchmark/empirical-study paper.

The comparison to the 'simultaneous' upper bound is somewhat restricted; a stronger natively continual baseline (e.g., replay- or distillation-based approaches adapted to unlearning) is not included, leaving open whether simpler alternatives could match the proposed add-ons.

strengths: The problem setting of continual (sequential) unlearning for text-to-image diffusion models is well-motivated and realistic, and the paper is among the first to systematically study it.
The paper is well organized, with a clear problem definition, metrics (UA, RA-I, RA-C), and a diagnostic narrative that connects utility collapse to cumulative parameter drift.

The empirical analysis includes several useful control experiments, e.g., matching optimization steps between sequential and simultaneous unlearning (Appendix D), curvature estimation to support the drift hypothesis (Appendix B), and interpolation analysis showing all-or-nothing erasure (Appendix C).
Generalization checks across two unlearning methods (ConAbl, SculpMem), an additional domain (celebrities), and an additional architecture (SDXL with ESD) strengthen the empirical claims.
The semantic-similarity correlation analysis (Figure 7) linking embedding proximity to retention degradation and cross-attention (k, v) distortion is a nice empirical insight.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the proposed 'contributions' are largely repurposed existing techniques applied to a new setting. L1/L2 norm regularization and selective fine-tuning are standard; model merging directly reuses TIES-Merging; the gradient-projection method is essentially gradient episodic memory / gradient projection memory (Chaudhry et al., 2018) with the subspace defined by CLIP text embeddings of LLM-generated auxiliary concepts. Lemma 7.1 is a trivial property of orthogonal projection, and the theoretical analysis (Section 5.2, Appendix B) is a standard second-order Taylor bound with Lipschitz-type constants — it formalizes intuition but does not yield new insight or precise predictions.

The empirical study is narrow: the benchmark is limited to one fine-tuned Stable Diffusion checkpoint, sequences of only 12 concepts from UnlearnCanvas (styles/objects) plus a small celebrity setting. It is unclear whether sequences were sampled once or across multiple random orders/seeds, and no variance or statistical significance is reported for the headline results.

Missing important baselines: despite explicitly framing the work via continual learning, the paper does not evaluate canonical continual-learning regularizers such as EWC, MAS, SI, or LoRA/adapters with task-arithmetic merging, nor simpler remedies like keeping a buffer of retention prompts for replay. The comparison set (L1/L2, SelFT, merge, projection) feels curated to favor the narrative.

Evaluation relies solely on fixed pretrained classifiers (UnlearnCanvas classifiers, GIPHY classifier). Classifier failure may not reflect true concept removal or true concept retention (e.g., a style classifier cannot verify that semantic content is intact), and no human evaluation or robustness to prompt paraphrase is provided.

The proposed methods substantially mitigate but do not solve the problem: retention accuracy still degrades to roughly 40–60% after 12 requests even with the best combinations, and the paper does not report the hyperparameter sensitivity (lambda, k%, number of auxiliary concepts M, LLM choice) on which the methods presumably depend.

Internal inconsistencies and presentation issues: the 'Project Page' link is empty, suggesting missing code/artifacts and weak reproducibility; several references have implausible future dates (Zhang et al., 2026; Mai et al., 2026), and Figure 12/13/15 axis labels appear cluttered and hard to read. Table 1 shows non-monotonic step counts (1300 for 4 concepts after 1200 for 3) that are unexplained.

The all-or-nothing erasure finding (Section 8) seems to undermine the paper's own merging approach (as the authors acknowledge), yet no remedy or deeper analysis is provided, weakening the practical guidance.

Significance is debatable: for a top-tier venue, the paper reads as a competent empirical study + application of known regularization recipes; the 'first systematic study' claim, while true to my knowledge, is paired with incremental technical content, and the authors explicitly disclaim proposing a new algorithm (Remark, Section 1), which limits the methodological contribution.

strengths: Identifies a genuinely underexplored and practically important problem: continual (sequential) unlearning for text-to-image diffusion models, where existing methods assume batch requests. The framing and three-part problem definition (erase new, preserve prior unlearning, retain unrelated abilities) are clear.

Well-designed empirical study with a clear diagnosis: the paper convincingly connects rapid utility collapse to cumulative parameter drift via controlled comparisons of sequential vs. simultaneous vs. independent unlearning (Figure 4), including a thoughtful control experiment showing drift is not merely an artifact of more optimization steps (Appendix D, Table 1).

The semantic-awareness analysis is a highlight: the strong negative correlation between retention accuracy and text-embedding similarity (Figure 7a), plus the mechanistic link to cross-attention K/V projections (Figure 7b), motivates the gradient-projection method in a principled rather than ad-hoc way.

Comprehensive evaluation coverage: two unlearning methods (ConAbl, SculpMem), three erasure domains (styles, objects, celebrities), an additional architecture (SDXL with ESD), and multiple metrics (UA, RA-I, RA-C, FID, CLIP score). The regularizers are shown to be complementary and combinable (Figures 8, 14, 17).

Useful additional analyses for the community: anchor-driven parameter updates ('unlearning is about learning', Figure 9), all-or-nothing erasure behavior under interpolation (Appendix C), and the practical efficiency comparison of sequential vs. simultaneous costs (Appendix E).
The paper is honest about scope (the Remark states it develops compatible add-ons rather than a new algorithm), and the plug-and-play nature of the regularizers increases practical applicability.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: L1/L2 norm penalties, selective fine-tuning, TIES-merging, and gradient projection are all well-established techniques from continual learning, pruning, model merging, and GEM-style optimization, largely transplanted to a new setting. The paper frames this as a strength (compatible add-ons), but the technical contribution is primarily empirical repackaging.

The theoretical analysis is thin: the Taylor-expansion bound is a standard argument, and Lemma 7.1 (first-order invariance) is essentially a one-line restatement of the definition of orthogonal projection. No treatment of second-order effects, which the projection method could still disturb.

The gradient-projection method depends on LLM-generated auxiliary concepts and CLIP text-embedding similarity, but there is no sensitivity analysis over the number of auxiliary concepts M, the similarity threshold, or failure modes when textual similarity poorly proxies visual/semantic similarity. Robustness of this key design choice is unverified.

Evaluation relies on a small number of generated images per concept (e.g., 5 seeds x 8 objects = 40 images per style concept), and classifier-based UA/RA metrics may be noisy or gameable; no confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are reported for the main comparisons.

Only two unlearning methods (ConAbl, SculpMem) are studied on the main benchmark, and ESD appears only in the SDXL/celebrity appendix setting; the generality of the collapse phenomenon and the remedies across a broader set of unlearning algorithms (e.g., ESD-x on SD v2, Salun, Rece) remains partially demonstrated.
Hyperparameter sensitivity (regularization strength lambda, top-k% in SelFT and TIES) and per-method compute/memory overhead of the add-ons are not systematically reported in the main text.

Several claims of being 'first' (first systematic study, first model merging for unlearning in text-to-image) should be softened given closely related concurrent work (e.g., Bui et al. 2024/2025 on cross-concept effects, which the authors do acknowledge in Appendix F.3).

Minor but noticeable quality issues: duplicate Gandikota et al. 2023a/b entries, suspicious future-dated citations (Zhang et al., 2026; Mai et al., 2026), and occasional inconsistencies that suggest insufficient proofreading.
